overview.title: About
overview.p1: Open Stream Environment is a Material Design 3 overlay plus a drag-and-drop control panel for Twitch and OBS. The overlay is served locally and added to OBS as a Browser Source.
overview.p2: Components: the overlay itself (shown in OBS), this control panel, standalone scenes, a standalone chat window (including one over the game), a Web Remote for phones and tablets, and an Elgato Stream Deck plugin.

quickstart.title: Quick start
quickstart.s1: Enable the WebSocket server in OBS (Tools → WebSocket Server Settings), then set the port and password in Settings → OBS WebSocket and turn the integration on — wait for the Connected status.
quickstart.s2: Press “Set up scenes in OBS”: the app creates the missing scenes and adds a browser source with the right URL and canvas size to each. Existing scenes and sources stay as they are, and pressing it again refreshes the URLs.
quickstart.s3: Add your gameplay capture to the main scene and move it below “OSE Overlay”: OBS puts new sources on top. Without the WebSocket, add the overlay source by hand — its address is in the “OBS Browser Source” panel of the editor.
quickstart.s4: In Settings → Twitch set at least your channel name (chat connects anonymously); optionally connect DonationAlerts and YouTube.
quickstart.s5: Arrange widgets in the editor: the Talk, Guests, Wheel and Poll scenes have their own layouts. Changes show up live.

editor.title: Editor
editor.p1: Drag widgets from the left library onto the canvas, or click one to add it.
editor.p2: Select a widget to edit its properties on the right. Drag to move it, use the corner handle to resize.
editor.p3: The Layers panel controls z-order; the Grid toggle helps with alignment. The “Set up scenes in OBS” button creates the sources for you; this URL is for adding a Browser Source by hand:
editor.p4: Widget icons appear on the canvas next to the label on hover or selection, so widgets are easier to tell apart.
editor.p5: The Lock button in the toolbar below the canvas prevents dragging, resizing, deleting, adding and reordering widgets. Selection and property editing stay available — handy for avoiding an accidental layout shift during a live stream.
editor.p6: For a 3D widget with an Angle slider the whole tile rotates on the canvas — frame, label and resize handles. Drag a handle along the widget's axes: width and height are measured in its rotated coordinate system, not on screen.

hud.title: Overlays over the game (HUD)
hud.p1: HUD edit mode (Settings → Application, default hotkey Control+Shift+H) opens the overlay over your game as a borderless window. Drag and resize widgets right in-game; the hotkey toggles the mode and the monitor is selected in settings.
hud.p2: Chat over game (Settings → Chat over game, default hotkey Control+Shift+L) shows the chat feed in a transparent window over your game. Clicks pass through, so it doesn't interfere with play — handy on a single monitor.
hud.p3: Chat settings cover the monitor, window size and position, background opacity and font size. X/Y are on-screen coordinates; leave them empty to dock the window to the top-right corner of the monitor.

widget.title: Custom widget
widget.p1: The widget library includes a Custom widget with several modes, switched in the properties panel on the right.
widget.p2: Text shows a title and text; Image shows an image URL; Video plays a file or link with fit, loop and sound; Custom HTML opens a separate HTML/CSS/JS editor with a live preview.
widget.p3: Embed (iframe) inserts a link to an external browser source (for example, a widget from DonationAlerts) as-is.
widget.p4: The video has no backdrop: WebM with an alpha channel (VP8/VP9) renders transparently right over the game. Loop repeats the clip, and Muted disables the audio track — muted video is always allowed to autoplay.

widgets.title: Widgets on the scene
widgets.p1: Every widget has its own settings in the inspector on the right. For the UEC transfer you can set the header channel, display duration, decode step (ms per character), and toggle the amount and message. Long text makes the panel grow by itself, up to the bottom of the screen.
widgets.p2: The UEC transfer shows event details: for a follow — that the contact is being watched, for a sub — the tier, for a gift — the number of gifted subs and the tier. The donation amount is coloured by tier, like in the TESO alert.
widgets.p3: The microphone visualizer has modes (sine, bars from the center, bars growing upward, spectrum envelope, ring), colour, opacity, gain and noise gate. Spectrum envelope is the same spectrum drawn as one smooth line filled downward: in a narrow strip it reads better than separate bars. Mirror flips the drawing across the vertical axis after rotation, so it means the same thing in any orientation. Rotate turns the drawing by 90° and swaps the frame sides — a vertical widget becomes tall, otherwise the wave would stay a strip in the centre. Direction flips the drawing the other way without touching the frame.
widgets.p4: The microphone visualizer, webcam frame, Recent events, 3D goals, the Executive Hangar timer, the built-in bubble of the DonateX AI character and the Donation music line have perspective: tilt strength 0–100 and a direction — left, right, up or down. The tilt is visible both in the overlay and in the editor preview. Every 3D widget also has an Angle slider (0–359°) that turns the widget within its own plane.
widgets.p5: Microphone settings are split in two: display (mode, color, opacity, perspective) is per widget, while the device, echo cancellation and noise suppression are global because the microphone is opened once. Under the device list you can see what is actually being captured: “Default” sometimes turns out to be a virtual input (NVIDIA Broadcast, cables) that produces silence. If the system default is like that, the panel picks the first physical microphone on its own — until a device is chosen manually.
widgets.p6: The webcam frame has two modes. Frame only is decoration: corners, a thin border and a LIVE badge in the current theme color; the camera is a separate OBS source. Live video from the panel makes the control panel capture the camera and send frames to the overlay; device, frame width, FPS (up to 60), codec, bitrate or JPEG quality are configurable, plus mirror and fit. H.264 through WebCodecs is used by default; if the browser or hardware cannot handle it, the panel falls back to JPEG. The OBS browser source itself has no camera access. The corner colour can be set separately from the frame (empty — taken from the theme), and the Neon toggle adds a glow around the frame and corners; the glow strength is 2–40 px.
widgets.p7: The news ticker is a scrolling line of stream events: donations, follows, subs, rewards, and optionally chat, the goal and the top donation. Speed is set in pixels per second and does not depend on message length; direction and sources are toggled in the inspector. There is a flat 2D variant and 3D tickers in the theme sets with a slight perspective. Ready-made phrases for it live in the Templates panel — send one into the ticker or the breaking bar in one click.
widgets.p8: 3D chats have a Show time toggle: it affects new messages only — chat keeps no history, just the rows on screen, so messages already shown keep their time. The TESO chat has no time at all.
widgets.p9: DonateX widgets — Donation music and the AI character — show what came with the donation: a single line with the track title, or a voiced reply. While there is no music, the line is not on screen at all. The inspector sets the queue and the character name: when donations arrive back to back, the next track or reply waits its turn instead of cutting off the current one. If the track link points to a YouTube page, there is no audio to play — the track stays for twenty seconds and then the widget takes the next one. The queue is controlled from the web remote: “Skip track” cuts the current track and takes the next one, “Stop” stops the player and clears the queue. If a donation ordered music, the alert also shows the track title — DonateX sends only the link, so the title comes from the YouTube video.
widgets.p10: The DonateX widget links — donation, AI character and music — are set in Settings → DonateX. They open hidden in the overlay: the service sees the widgets as connected and plays the sound itself, while OSE draws the picture. Our music widget then shows the title and does not duplicate the sound.
widgets.p11: The music widget link makes DonateX the owner of the queue: our line shows whatever track its page is playing, even if the donation arrived earlier or the track was queued in the service dashboard. Titles for YouTube links come from the video itself. The line stays while the music plays and disappears when the service stops the queue — it has no twenty-second timer. If the widget is tilted or the theme runs in 3D, it fades in and out.

guests.title: Guest cameras
guests.p1: In Settings → Guest cameras each slot has an Invite button: it creates a one-time ose-join:// link.
guests.p2: Send the link to the guest. They paste it into OSE, enter a name and wait — the camera starts only after you press Allow. The link lives for 15 minutes and survives a dropped connection.
guests.p3: In the layout pick the camera widget, the Guest camera source and a slot. Up to four slots give up to four guest cameras in frame; each volume is adjusted in the properties. The “Guest name on the badge” toggle shows the connected guest's name on the frame, and the usual “LIVE” label while nobody is connected. Guest audio is off by default (“Video only”): the guest can stay in Discord and their microphone will not reach the stream — turn the sound on in the properties if you need it.
guests.p4: An invite can be created for the internet (through a signaling service) or for the local network. For the guest's voice to reach the stream, enable “Control audio via OBS” on the Browser Source. The signaling address is set in Settings; see signal/README.md for deploying your own service.
guests.p5: The slot is assigned automatically: a new widget with the Guest camera source gets the first free one, and slots already chosen are left alone. Without a slot the widget shows No slot selected and accepts no stream — change it by hand only to pin a guest to a specific place.
guests.p6: The video goes directly over WebRTC: the internet invite travels through the signaling service, but the video itself never reaches it. STUN servers are built in — they help both sides learn their public addresses. If someone sits behind a strict NAT (mobile internet, some providers), a TURN server is required: the host enters its address, user and password in Settings, and the guest receives them with the confirmation. With TURN the video is relayed through its server, so you need your own or a rented one.
guests.p7: Both roles can run at once: host your own guest and be a guest on several other streamers' channels. Your camera goes out through the outgoing connections while guests come into your overlay; identical slot names (cam2 on both sides, for example) do not interfere.
guests.p8: You can hold several connections: paste the next invite and press Connect again — each connection gets its own row in My connections and its own Disconnect button. That is how a mesh is built: with four participants each of them invites the other three and accepts three invites. The camera is captured once but encoded separately for each host, so outgoing traffic and load grow with the number of connections; the limit is four.
guests.p9: If the internet invite connects but the picture stays black, the sides failed to traverse NAT and a TURN server is needed. There is no bundled relay and automatic credentials are not implemented yet — the fields in Settings are only for your own server. The simplest option is coturn on a VPS: open TCP and UDP 3478 and UDP 49152–65535; in /etc/turnserver.conf set listening-port=3478, lt-cred-mech, realm=ose, user=ose:password, external-ip with your address, and min-port/max-port from the same range; start turnserver and check the address on icetest.info. In Settings enter turn:ADDRESS:3478?transport=udp (and also turn:ADDRESS:3478?transport=tcp if UDP is blocked), with the login and password from user=. Without your own TURN, a group of friends can use a VPN network (Radmin VPN, ZeroTier): a Local network invite with host= replaced by the address in that network works as if everyone were on one LAN.

presets.title: Layout presets
presets.p1: The Presets block in the toolbar under the canvas saves the current widget layout under a name for quick layout switching.
presets.p2: A preset also saves the active 2D/3D themes, so loading one brings back its 3D widgets automatically.
presets.p3: Save overwrites the selected preset or creates a new one from the entered name; Delete removes a preset. Presets live in local-db.json and don't touch other settings.

pollpresets.title: Poll presets
pollpresets.p1: In the left column of the Poll panel you can save the current configuration (command, chart type and options) as a named preset.
pollpresets.p2: Selecting a preset in the list loads its options, command and chart type. Save overwrites the selected preset or creates a new one from the entered name; Delete removes it. Presets live in local-db.json.

packages.title: Widget and theme packages
packages.p1: A widget or theme can be installed as a folder in the packages directory: %APPDATA%\com.openstreamenvironment.app\plugins\<id>\ (in development — config/plugins/<id>/). Restart the app after installing: manifests are read at startup.
packages.p2: A widget is described by widget.json — name, code file, styles, default size and a settings schema. It appears as its own card in the library, and the inspector renders fields from the schema. A theme is described by theme.json — a token set and optional CSS; it appears in the theme list as plugin:<id>.
packages.p3: Package code runs in the overlay page with full permissions, so install only trusted packages. See docs/plugin-api.md and docs/examples/plugins/ for the manifest format and examples.

themes.title: Themes
themes.p1: In Settings → Appearance each theme is a "family" with a base 2D palette and, for some, a 3D variant: Material You, Orbital (a Star Citizen HUD), Pixel Perfect (a minimal pixel-style UI), Elite (an orange Elite Dangerous HUD), Nuclear (a CRT terminal), TESO (dark gold/bronze, Cinzel/Montserrat fonts), Wardogs (a tactical shooter HUD with an amber accent) and Super Four (a Honda CB400SF motorcycle dashboard: pearl violet, Candy Flash pink and cyan stripes, Showa gold, a tachometer).
themes.p2: The 3D toggle on a theme card turns on its 3D widgets over the same palette: Material You → orb, chat, goal and alert, Pixel Perfect → cube, chat, goal and alert, Orbital → Star Citizen (Grim HEX), Elite → Cobra Mk II (ship hologram and radar where donors appear as ships), Nuclear → radiation sign, chat, goal and holo-alert, TESO → Ouroboros Seal, chat, goal and holo-alert, Wardogs → a goal loading bar, chat, holo-alert and a wireframe cube, Super Four → tachometer (revs rise with chat activity, spikes on alerts), chat, goal, alert and a wireframe cube.
themes.p3: When 3D is on, its widgets appear over the base overlay and the matching 2D widgets (chat, goal, alerts) are hidden — their 3D versions replace them; switching 3D off brings them back. An active 3D theme also shows a "3D widgets" list below, where each widget can be toggled individually. The theme only affects the overlay and its canvas preview.
themes.p4: Create custom theme and Edit open a full theme editor in a separate window: 4 seed colors, seven panel shapes, separate fonts for headings/body/data, border, glow, background and text color, panel opacity and blur, error color and alert enter animation (duration and curve), plus a CSS editor. Pixel Perfect snaps widget text to the pixel grid (12/16/24/32px).
themes.p5: A custom theme shows a list of every 3D widget (Material You, Star Citizen/Grim HEX, Nuclear, Pixel Perfect, TESO, Cobra Mk II, Wardogs, Retrowave, Super Four) with toggles — pick any, styles can be mixed. The "3D" toggle on its card enables the selection; panel 3D widgets use your palette, while decorative signs/radar/shield keep their signature colors. If exactly one widget is ticked for a role (chat/goal/alerts) the 2D widget is replaced by it automatically; with several it stays as is.

scenes.title: Scenes
scenes.p1: Each scene is a separate OBS source that replaces the gameplay view entirely (not drawn on top of it).
scenes.p2: Available scenes: Start, BRB, Main, Just Chatting, Guests, End, Fortune Wheel, Poll and Pause.
scenes.p3: Just Chatting shows a large chat feed and alerts, leaving room for your webcam on the left.
scenes.p4: The “Set up scenes in OBS” button in the OBS WebSocket settings creates the sources for the scenes — it puts the right URL into each one. You can still copy a scene's URL manually in the “OBS Browser Source” panel on the right of the editor. Switch scenes from the remote or Stream Deck. Each scene can show a banner (title, subtitle, socials, recent events) and a countdown timer.
scenes.p5: Scenes have a countdown timer: enable Timer, set the duration in seconds and the text shown when it ends. It starts when the scene is activated, survives an OBS browser-source reload and is not reset by settings changes; when entering through a splash it starts after the splash finishes.
scenes.p6: The Guests scene is for talking with guests: four guest frames in a two-by-two grid with chat on the right. The frames are bound to multicam slots, so a participant invited in Settings → Guest cameras appears in their own tile without editing the layout; the name and frame are set in the widget inspector.

splashes.title: Splashes
splashes.p1: A splash is a video, image or GIF played during scene transitions: when entering BRB, Talk, End, Wheel and Poll, and when returning to gameplay from these scenes or from Start (the stream intro).
splashes.p2: Configured on the Splashes tab: one file for all scenes plus a file and duration per scene. Priority: the scene's file → the global file → the standard brand splash (when no file is set). The standard splash follows the active theme.
splashes.p3: Duration is auto or 1–30 seconds: video always plays to the end, while an image/GIF with auto holds the default time. The switch to the target scene happens automatically — on the video's end or on the timer.
splashes.p4: Every scene has a toggle: a disabled scene skips its splash and switches immediately. It affects both entering the scene and returning from it to gameplay.
splashes.p5: Playback needs an OBS scene "Opening" with the http://localhost:8710/overlay/video-splash.html browser source (copy the link on the Splashes tab); the scene name is set in Settings → OBS WebSocket → Opening. The “Set up scenes in OBS” button creates this scene and source itself and leaves “Shutdown source when not visible” off; if you added the source manually, turn that checkbox off — otherwise the splash may not connect in time, and loading mid-splash replays it. If the Opening scene is missing, the transition goes straight to the target scene.
splashes.p6: Below you can set a background for each scene — video or image behind the card and widgets. Empty — the blurred theme background. For pause this is the only place to set it.

hotkeys.title: Hotkeys
hotkeys.p1: Global hotkeys work even when the game has focus. The first two are changed in Settings → Application (format like Control+Shift+H); on macOS use Command instead of Control.
hotkeys.p2: Control+Shift+H — HUD edit mode: a transparent overlay appears over the game, widgets can be dragged and resized, and the grid/snap turns on.
hotkeys.p3: Control+Shift+L — chat over the game: a transparent chat window that stays above other windows and passes clicks through (handy on a single monitor).
hotkeys.p4: Control+Shift+C — pin/unpin the chat window (always on top). Control+Shift+G — game mode: hide or show the control panel so it doesn't get in the way on stream. Control+Shift+K — turn the camera off/on: panel capture stops, widgets show a placeholder, and the OBS webcam source is muted when configured.

twitch.title: Twitch
twitch.p1: Chat connects anonymously and only needs the channel name.
twitch.p2: For follow/sub/cheer alerts you need a Twitch application and authorization.
twitch.p3: You can send chat messages from the Chat window and Web Remote — they are posted as the streamer via Twitch Helix (scope user:write:chat), so sending requires the authorization described below.
twitch.s2: Set the Redirect URI to the value shown in Settings → Twitch.
twitch.s3: Paste the Client ID and Client Secret.
twitch.s4: Press Connect Twitch and approve the authorization in the browser.

chatbot.title: Chat bot and moderation
chatbot.p1: In Settings → Chat bot you can enable the bot, set the command prefix and add your own commands (responses support $(user), $(channel), $(args), $(count), $(random a|b|c)) and timers. Each command has an access level (everyone / subscribers / moderators / broadcaster), a global cooldown and a per-user cooldown. The built-in !commands command lists the commands available to the viewer.
chatbot.p2: The bot can only reply when Twitch is connected with the user:write:chat scope — messages are posted as the channel via Twitch Helix.
chatbot.p3: The Moderation section enables auto moderation: link protection (with an allowed-domain whitelist), a blocked-word list with de-leetization of lookalike characters, caps and emote limits, and cumulative warnings: first offense clears the message and warns, second times out, third bans.
chatbot.p4: Timeouts and bans require the additional moderator:manage:banned_users scope — reconnect Twitch. In the terminal, the modtest <message> command checks a message without actually banning.

donationalerts.title: DonationAlerts
donationalerts.p1: Donations automatically increase the goal counter and trigger an alert.
donationalerts.p2: Donation voice-over (TTS): in the DonationAlerts card you can enable reading the donation message aloud — language, voice, volume and speech rate, plus a test button. If the service returns a voice link, the DonationAlerts voice can also be used for regular donations (a separate toggle).
donationalerts.p3: The DA button in the top bar opens a pair of panels: DonationAlerts itself and, to its left, the alert queue. They open and close together and share one close button: the queue shows what is on air and what is waiting, and lets you pause alerts and set the display rules — hide donations below an amount and merge consecutive donations from the same viewer.
donationalerts.s2: Set the Redirect URI to the value shown in Settings → DonationAlerts.
donationalerts.s3: Paste the Client ID and Client Secret, then press Connect DonationAlerts.

youtube.title: YouTube
youtube.p1: Live chat and live events (Super Chat, new members) via the YouTube Data API v3.
youtube.s1: Create an OAuth client in console.cloud.google.com.
youtube.s2: Enable the YouTube Data API v3 for the project.
youtube.s3: Set the Redirect URI shown in Settings → YouTube and paste the Client ID/Secret.
youtube.s4: Connect, then optionally set a Video ID as a fallback for live-chat lookup.

obs.title: OBS WebSocket
obs.p1: Requires OBS 28+ with the WebSocket server enabled (Tools → WebSocket Server Settings).
obs.p2: Scene mapping translates logical remote names into your actual OBS scene names. The fields suggest names from the connected OBS, and letter case does not matter: “brb” finds the “BRB” scene.
obs.p3: You can also define custom RAW commands, camera angles (multicam) and camera filters, triggered by Twitch points or manually.
obs.p4: The Camera and Microphone fields set the sources for the webcam and microphone toggle buttons in the remote.
obs.p5: The “Set up scenes in OBS” button creates the missing scenes and browser sources for you; it is enabled only while the WebSocket is connected.
obs.p6: What the button sets up: a source sized to the canvas in the top-left corner, locked against accidental dragging, with “Shutdown source when not visible” on every source except the splash. Existing scenes and sources are never deleted or renamed (names are compared case-insensitively), and pressing the button again refreshes the URLs after a port change. The button does not create gameplay capture: add it to the main scene yourself.
obs.s1: Enable the WebSocket server in OBS: Tools → WebSocket Server Settings.
obs.s2: Enter the port and password here, turn the integration on and wait for the Connected status.
obs.s3: Press “Set up scenes in OBS” and confirm — the scenes and sources appear in OBS.
obs.s4: Add your gameplay capture source to the main scene (Main in the mapping) and move it below “OSE Overlay”: OBS puts new sources on top, and the capture would cover the overlay.

soundboard.title: Soundboard
soundboard.p1: Map a Twitch channel-points reward to a sound file and an image/GIF animation.
soundboard.p2: Adjust the volume and queue mode, then test each sound from the panel.

rewards.title: Channel rewards (actions)
rewards.p1: In Settings → Channel rewards (actions) a Twitch channel-points reward is mapped to actions: show an alert, speak a phrase (TTS) and/or switch a scene. You can use {user}, {reward} and {input} (the text the viewer enters when redeeming).
rewards.p2: One reward can trigger several actions at once. Twitch must be connected with the channel:read:redemptions scope. Test with the ▶ button or the sim points <name> terminal command.

clipmarker.title: Clip & stream marker
clipmarker.p1: The Clip and Marker buttons live in the app header — they create a Twitch clip and marker via the Helix API in one click.
clipmarker.p2: A clip needs the clips:edit scope, a marker needs channel:manage:broadcast. If the buttons report an error, reconnect Twitch in Settings — the old token doesn't include the new scopes.

streamdeck.title: Stream Deck
streamdeck.p1: The Elgato plugin switches scenes: Start, BRB, Wheel, Talk and End.
streamdeck.p2: Set custom per-scene icons in Settings → Stream Deck.

remote.title: Web Remote
remote.p1: Open from a phone or tablet on the same Wi-Fi network using the address shown in the header.
remote.p2: From the remote you can switch scenes, control the wheel and death counter, send test alerts, skip and stop Donation music tracks, run OBS commands, change the theme, switch cameras, trigger effects and send chat messages.
remote.p3: The Wheel tab holds the wheel settings (command, participants, list position, volume, speed) and the participant list: add and remove viewers right from the remote.
remote.p4: Next to the webcam there is a microphone mute button — set the audio input name in Settings → OBS.
remote.p5: The Chat tab has an input at the bottom — you can not only follow the message feed but also send your own messages to Twitch chat.
remote.p6: The remote address carries an access code, and that code is the pass into the local network. The panel, the OBS overlay and the HUD work from this computer without it, while anything over the network — a phone, third-party scripts — cannot connect without it. If the address leaked, press “New access code” in Settings → “Network access”.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.p1: When someone follows, subscribes, gifts a sub, donates or cheers, a popup card appears in the top-right corner of the control panel. It disappears on its own after a few seconds.
notifications.p2: If the panel is minimized to tray or out of focus, a native Windows toast notification is shown instead of the in-panel card.
notifications.p3: The notification sound (buzzer.wav) and its volume are configured in Settings → Application: the Notification sound toggle and Notification volume slider.

terminal.title: Terminal and commands
terminal.p1: The Terminal button in the header opens the built-in console: it shows server and integration logs in real time.
terminal.p2: Type commands in the input (e.g. scene brb, death +1, wheel spin, sim sub user, theme pixel, status). Type help for the full list.
terminal.p3: Tab autocompletes commands and arguments (scenes, sounds, cameras, filters). The search field in the terminal header filters logs by text, and logs <level> filters by level.

templates.title: Templates
templates.p1: The Templates button in the header opens a panel with ready-made phrases for the news ticker. Type into the New template field and press Add — the phrase is saved in settings and survives a restart.
templates.p2: Each row has two buttons: To ticker puts the phrase into the common event flow, To breaking shows it as a separate bar above the ticker without waiting for the cycle to end. Edits happen right in the row; an empty row and a duplicate remove themselves.
templates.p3: Up to 20 phrases of 200 characters each are stored. The same message can be sent from the terminal with ticker [breaking] <text> or from the Web Remote.
templates.p4: Each template has Pause and Remove next to the send buttons. Pause hides the announcement in the ticker without deleting it: other events keep going, and Resume brings it back. Remove deletes it from the ticker until the next send. Clear announcements removes all announcements at once, while Pause ticker stops the whole line without clearing events and is saved in settings.

wheel.title: Fortune Wheel
wheel.p1: Viewers join by typing the entry command in Twitch chat.
wheel.p2: Elimination mode removes one participant per spin until the final winner.
wheel.p3: The Wheel button in the header opens the wheel settings panel, with a participants panel (search and clear) next to it.
wheel.p4: Use Generate wheel and Spin the wheel, plus the music and sound volume and spin speed settings.
wheel.p5: In the Web Remote, the Wheel tab mirrors these settings and lets you manage participants from your phone.

debug.title: Debug
debug.p1: The Debug button in the header opens a panel with test buttons: alerts (follow, sub, gift, cheer, donation) and a test chat.
debug.p2: Integration debug logs (such as heartbeat events) are shown below. Use Clear to remove accumulated logs.

history.title: History & data
history.p1: The History button in the top bar opens a window with three tabs: Events, Sessions and Chat.
history.p2: Events lists donations, subscriptions, follows and cheers with search, a type filter and a Replay button. The current selection can be exported to CSV/JSON or deleted by filter.
history.p3: Sessions lists your streams: start time, channel, duration and how many events/donations/messages each stream had.
history.p4: Chat shows saved chat messages with search. Recording is enabled with the Store chat history toggle in Settings → Data & storage.
history.p5: With the panel open, keys 1, 2 and 3 switch tabs (Events / Sessions / Chat), and Esc closes the panel.

performance.title: Performance
performance.p1: Set the overlay Browser Source FPS to 30 in OBS: widgets never animate faster anyway (3D at 20–30, the mic visualizer at 30), while 60 only doubles the work.
performance.shutdown: The “Set up scenes in OBS” button enables it for you. For a source added by hand, enable “Shutdown source when not visible”: without this checkbox Chromium inside OBS may not set document.hidden for an inactive scene, so the rAF pause of 3D widgets won't kick in and the hidden scene keeps rendering.
performance.p2: Keep “Refresh browser when scene becomes active” off — a reload resets animations and delays the picture. The scene setup button leaves it off.
performance.p3: Only animated 3D widgets are heavy: radar, hologram, sign/billboard, shield, orb/cube. Each runs its own canvas loop; 2–3 at a time is comfortable, and don't stretch them across the whole screen.
performance.p4: 2D widgets (chat, goal, recent events, counter, social banner, participants) are cheap — you can have many. During a hype, shrink the chat box: 3D-theme HUD chats keep up to 50 rows.
performance.p5: Keep a single mic visualizer: the 30 Hz mic capture runs only while that widget is on a scene and stops when it is removed.
performance.p6: A custom widget with arbitrary JS is potentially the most expensive — watch the timers in your own code. Check the load in OBS (View → Stats).
performance.p7: The Executive Hangar timer is the app's only outbound request: it calls the Longshot API every 5 minutes (and via the “Refresh” button) and only while a visible timer is in the layout. Hide or remove the widget and polling stops.

settings.title: Application settings
settings.p1: Port changes the local server port and requires an app restart.
settings.p2: Appearance manages overlay themes; Export/Import saves the full config.json together with media files (it contains secrets — don't share it).
settings.p3: Language switches the whole interface between English and Russian.
settings.p4: The event notification sound and its volume are configured in the Application card (the Notification sound toggle and Notification volume slider).
settings.p5: Base currency is the currency of the stream total. Donations in other currencies are converted at the rate loaded at startup and refreshed every twelve hours; without a rate the amount is shown on a separate line. The donation goal keeps its own currency in the widget properties.

updates.title: Updates
updates.p1: On startup the app checks for an update (without downloading) and, if one is available, highlights the Update button in the header.
updates.p2: Click Update to open a small menu with Later or Update. Update downloads and installs the new version; Later closes the menu. You can also press Check for updates in Settings → Application: if an update is found, the same button becomes Update and restart, and if not, it shows No updates available next to it. In dev mode (npm start) auto-update is unavailable and only works in packaged builds.

data.title: Data and backups
data.p1: Exporting settings saves the full config.json plus all files from the media folder (sounds, images, GIFs) in a single file.
data.p2: On import, media files are automatically restored into the media folder.
data.p3: The media cleanup command in the terminal removes unused media files. Window sizes and positions are remembered, and server logs are written to the logs folder.
data.p4: The Data & storage card shows the data folder path, database and history sizes, the session count, and lets you set the event history limit, clear data by scope and open the folder with the files.
